Ozonolysis. An organic chemical reaction that uses ozone to cleave the unsaturated carbon-carbon double or triple bonds of alkenes or alkynes. By breaking both the sigma and pi bonds, the reaction splits the carbon skeleton to produce carbonyl compounds—such as aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids—depending on the starting material's structure and the reaction workup conditions.

The reaction proceeds via a molozonide intermediate, an unstable one-point-two-point-three-trioxolane formed by a three-plus-two cycloaddition of ozone across the double bond, which quickly rearranges into a more stable one-point-two-point-four-trioxolane called an ozonide. The reaction utilizes a reductive workup using dimethyl sulfide or zinc dust in acid to cleave the ozonide intermediate, yielding aldehydes and ketones as the final products. Alternatively, an oxidative workup uses hydrogen peroxide to convert the ozonide, which oxidizes any potential aldehyde products into carboxylic acids while leaving ketones intact.

Historically, ozonolysis served as a primary analytical tool to determine the position of double bonds in unknown organic compounds by analyzing the resulting carbonyl fragments. When the reaction cleaves alkynes, it yields carboxylic acids or acid anhydrides directly, without requiring an oxidative workup.

Ozone, the triatomic allotrope of oxygen, serves as the highly reactive electrophilic cleaving agent. Metallic zinc is a common reducing agent used to decompose the ozonide intermediate during workup. Reductive ozonolysis of terminal or monosubstituted alkenes yields aldehydes.
